Phase 0 diagnostic · Alpamayo 1.5 & 2 Super · PAI-AV OOD reasoning split

Does the trajectory actually depend on the reasoning?

Alpamayo emits a Chain-of-Causation explanation and then a driving trajectory. If the reasoning is doing work, deleting it should make the true trajectory less likely.

What is being computed

The quantity is a conditional pointwise mutual information — how much more probable the model considers the actual future trajectory once it can read its own reasoning, holding the scene fixed. Nothing is trained or sampled; the ground-truth trajectory is teacher-forced and we read the model's own likelihood for it.

LLR  =  log p(a* | v, ℓ)  −  log p(a* | v)
a*
The ground-truth future trajectory the vehicle actually drove — 6.4 s, discretized to 128 tokens.
ℓ
The gold human-annotated Chain-of-Causation text for that event (e.g. “Stop for the pedestrian crossing ahead”), not the model's own generated reasoning.
v
The scene: camera frames at the event timestamp, plus the ego vehicle's own motion history.

Both terms come from a single teacher-forced forward pass each. The model's next-token cross-entropy over exactly the trajectory-token span is −log p(a* | context), so the two passes differ only in whether the reasoning is present in the prompt:

Numerator — reasoning present
The gold CoC sits in its normal place in the sequence.
[ images · ego history · prompt · reasoning · trajectory ]
Denominator — reasoning absent
The reasoning text is removed, leaving its block structure intact. This is the cleanest available denominator, but it is not a configuration the model is comfortable in — see the caveat on the empty control below.
[ images · ego history · prompt · — · trajectory ]

Three structural controls run through the same scoring path return exactly 0.0000 — re-scoring an identical sequence, re-tokenizing from scratch, and the trajectory-history tokens, which precede the reasoning and so cannot depend on it under causal attention. They are the alignment check: a probe that is misaligned cannot return exact zeros on all three.

Reading the units

Nats per trajectory token; one bit is 0.69 nats. A positive value means the reasoning makes the true trajectory more likely; zero means the trajectory distribution is unchanged by it. The trajectory is tokenized as 64 waypoints × (acceleration, curvature) at dt = 0.1 s, interleaved, which is what lets the result be resolved by horizon time and by control channel further down.

What a nat is worth here

The numbers below are small, so it helps to fix the scale first. Score the true trajectory against a foreign one — another event’s future, a median 17 metres away — under identical conditioning. That gap is what the model gains from knowing which trajectory is actually right, and it is the natural yardstick for everything else on this page.

Referencenats / tokenshare
knowing which trajectory is right+0.7748100%
the cameras — swap in another event’s camera frames, keep everything else+0.266134%
every reasoning effect measured here±0.0004 to +0.0180.05% to 2%

So a tenth of a nat is a large quantity in this study, and a hundredth is not. The full breakdown, once each effect has been introduced, is in Every effect as a share of the separation further down.

Most events land within ±0.02 nats of zero

Per-event means over 128 trajectory tokens each; 23 of 2,071 events fall outside ±0.2 and are not drawn. Mean +0.0010, median +0.0021, 10% trimmed mean +0.0029, std 0.0509, range −0.327 to +0.259. The distribution is left-skewed, so the plain mean sits below the other two. Later sections quote the trimmed figure, which is why this same quantity appears there as +0.0029 rather than +0.0010. Split separately: train +0.0006 (n=1,722), val +0.0030 (n=349).

No effect at any horizon, in either control channel

The overall number could be zero while the effect is real in one part of the trajectory. There are two places to check. The first is the prediction horizon: vision and ego-motion predict the next half-second well, so if reasoning helps anywhere it should be further out, where those run out. The second is the two control channels: a CoC that says “stop for the pedestrian” should move acceleration, and one that says “merge left” should move curvature.

The result is flat in both. Across all eight time bins the LLR stays within ±0.007 nats, with no trend toward the long horizon, and the two channels come out at −0.0001 (acceleration) and +0.0021 (curvature).

Gridlines are drawn at a hundredth of a nat — the vision-replaced control would sit 26× above the top of this chart. Channel totals over all 265,088 scored tokens: acceleration −0.0001, curvature +0.0021.

The pattern across the twelve: the most-positive and most-negative events are not distinguishable by scenario type, by what the reasoning says, or by whether the trajectory does anything unusual. Several of the strongest positives are routine decelerations that the ego-motion history already predicts; several of the strongest negatives carry reasoning that describes the manoeuvre correctly. That is what a null looks like at the level of individual examples.

Tail scenes regress to the mean under any change

The twelve scenes above were picked from the two ends of the distribution, which makes them tempting to read as cases where the reasoning did or did not work. They cannot be read that way.

These events were selected for being extreme, and a selected extreme regresses toward the mean under any perturbation. Re-scoring the same scenes against a hundred unrelated donor CoCs each gives the regression directly:

Scene bucketown reasoning mean over 100 donorsshift
Most negative−0.308−0.200+0.108
At the mean+0.001−0.000−0.001
Most positive+0.253+0.188−0.065

Arbitrary prose lifts the bottom, drops the top, and leaves the middle untouched — and it does so by more than the reversed-directive panels on the cards above move those same scenes (+0.108 against +0.039 at the bottom; −0.065 against −0.015 at the top). A reversed directive is still topically about its scene, so it stays closer to the gold text than a stranger’s prose does. A directive flip on a tail-selected event measures the selection, not the model, so nothing in either direction should be read as evidence about how the model treats directives. The flips worth reading are the ones on the middle cards, which carry no selection: they move the likelihood by −0.0003, −0.0021 and +0.0047 — nothing.

The same twelve buckets on Alpamayo 2 Super

Selected the same way, on A2S's own corrected values, and shown with its native six-camera profile. The tails span a similar range (−0.33 to +0.34), which is the point worth noticing: the per-event spread is comparable between the two models, and what differs is where the distribution is centred — 1.5 sits on zero, A2S sits at +0.018. Individual extremes are not what distinguishes a model that uses its reasoning from one that doesn't; the mean over two thousand events is.

Does it matter what the reasoning says, or only that it is there?

The measurement so far deletes the reasoning and sees what happens. That answers one question but hides another. Deleting the reasoning removes two things at once: the words, and the fact that anything was there at all. Those are not the same, and only one of them is about reasoning.

A reasoning block raises the likelihood even when its contents are worthless. Replace the prose with pad tokens — same length, no information — and roughly 72% of the effect survives on the four largest events, and 96% on the largest (+0.2490 against gold’s +0.2594). So a positive result does not show the model read anything. It can just mean the model had thirteen more positions to compute over, which is a known effect in language models.

To separate the two, the reasoning needs to be replaced rather than deleted — swapped for another event’s real reasoning, which is fluent, the right kind of text, and wrong about this scene. Averaged over several such donors, that gives a second comparison:

gold − empty
Does having reasoning there at all help?
gold − donor
Does it help that the reasoning is about this scene, rather than being any fluent prose of the same length?

Both comparisons have now been run over the full split: 2,071 events, the same events for each, with log p(gold) bit-identical between the two runs.

Reasoning there vs not · gold − empty
+0.0029
10% trimmed · 54.4% of events positive, sign p=6.3e−5
This scene’s reasoning vs another’s · gold − donor
−0.0004
10% trimmed · Wilcoxon p=0.99

Read those two numbers with care, because the plain average lies here — in both directions. A few events sit far out in the left tail, and an average of 2,071 values is easily dragged by them. On the second comparison the plain average is −0.0037, which looks like a real effect and would mean the correct reasoning is worse than a stranger’s. It is not. The middle of the distribution is slightly positive, the trimmed average is −0.0004, and a rank test gives p = 0.99 — no shift at all. The same skew works the other way on the first comparison, where the plain average understates an effect that rank tests put solidly above zero.

So the reasoning’s content does nothing. Another event’s prose works exactly as well as the prose written for this scene. Having something in the slot is worth a small but reliable amount — about 0.15% of the baseline likelihood, roughly 1% of what the camera feed is worth. What this diagnostic measures is a filled slot, not reasoning. That is what the pad-token result predicted, now confirmed on two thousand events rather than four.

The same holds on Alpamayo 2 Super. Its presence term is eighteen times larger (+0.0171 trimmed, p = 3×10−70) and entirely robust — but its content term, measured the same way over 2,070 events, is also zero (+0.0003 trimmed, p = 0.58). The two models differ in magnitude, not in kind: neither trajectory head uses what its reasoning says.

It also sharpens what a regularizer has to beat. The target is not a flat zero but an occupancy-only baseline, and the dependence it needs to create is specifically a dependence on content.

One hypothesis for the tail events was tested and rejected: that the model rewards prose which is merely typical of its training distribution. Correlation between per-token prose likelihood and the LLR is r = +0.218, and deliberately nonsensical prose at −14.44 nats per token still retains 70% of the effect. Typicality does not explain it.

Longer reasoning gives a bigger effect, but only across scenes

If the presence term is extra positions to compute over rather than anything about reasoning, then a longer reasoning span should buy more. It does, on both models, monotonically.

1.5 · shortest quartile
−0.0041
median 12 CoC tokens
1.5 · longest quartile
+0.0080
median 22 CoC tokens
A2S · shortest
+0.0070
median 10 tokens
A2S · longest
+0.0220
median 20 tokens

On Alpamayo 1.5 the shortest quartile is negative and the longest is twice the overall mean (Pearson r = +0.127, p = 7×10−9; A2S r = +0.110, p = 5×10−7). Since the content term is zero, a length effect cannot be “longer reasoning says more”. It is tokens in the span buying likelihood — the pause-token effect, measured directly.

The donor comparison makes the same point more sharply, because there the two sides differ in length by a known amount. Plotting the gold-vs-donor LLR against len(gold) − len(donor) gives a straight line through the origin:

The slope is +0.00122 nats per token on 1.5 (7.0σ) and +0.00158 on A2S (8.8σ) — the steeper slope on the model with the larger presence term, as it should be. The 1.5 slope independently reproduces the quartile numbers above, which imply 0.0121/10 = 0.0012 per token from a completely separate cut of the data.

The intercept is the cleanest content estimate in this study, and it is zero in both models. Where the gold and donor spans are the same length, the LLR is −0.0036 on 1.5 and −0.0025 on A2S. Restricting to the ~410 events per model with |Δ| ≤ 1 gives trimmed means of −0.0021 (p = 0.13) and −0.0010 (p = 0.42). Neither is distinguishable from zero.

So the content null is not an artefact of unmatched donor lengths — it survives holding length fixed. The two models agree, and differ only in how strongly the length relation applies.

But this regression is across scenes, and it does not survive holding the scene fixed. Every point above is a different event, so CoC length is confounded with scene difficulty and with how verbose an annotator was — which is the likely reason the fit explains only 2–4% of the variance. Re-running it within a scene — same images, same target trajectory, a hundred donor CoCs of naturally varying length — removes that confound by construction. The per-scene slopes, six of eight individually significant, are:

Scenemin1min2min3 mean1mean2mean3max1 max2
nats / token+0.0043+0.0171 −0.0277−0.0003−0.0000 −0.0004+0.0023+0.0240

They disagree in sign and span an order of magnitude. Pooled with scene fixed effects the estimate is +0.0028 nats/token, but it explains 1.3% of the within-scene variance and it is not stable — on the first four scenes it was −0.0007, and adding four more flipped its sign. So “tokens in the span buy likelihood” is an across-scene regularity, not a within-scene mechanism. Individual scenes do respond strongly to reasoning length, but they respond in different directions, and the average of those responses is roughly nothing.

Meaningless filler does as well as real reasoning

The length results above all vary real prose, so “longer” and “says more” are never fully separated. This test separates them: hold the scene and the target trajectory fixed, put n tokens of meaningless filler in the reasoning block, and vary n. Filler cannot say more as it gets longer, so any effect is from the token count alone. Two kinds of filler were used: a repeated ordinary word, and the pad token. 70 scenes, fourteen values of n.

Mean LLR against an empty reasoning block; 70 scenes, scene and target trajectory held fixed, so only the number of filler positions varies. Shaded band and dashed vertical: the mean ± 1 sd of real CoC length over all 2,077 annotated events (14.9 ± 4.2 tokens). The peak sits just beyond it, at 24 tokens.

The first 32 tokens on a linear axis, shaded to ±1 standard error over the 70 scenes. The repeated word is above zero from one token onward. The pad token dips below zero between 4 and 8 tokens before recovering — padding inside a reasoning block is a sequence the model never saw in training. Gold’s band spans zero.

The curve is an inverted U. Filler helps up to about 24 tokens, then starts to hurt. At 16–32 tokens the repeated word is worth +0.008 to +0.011 (Wilcoxon p = 0.005 and 0.014). Past 64 tokens both fillers go negative, reaching −0.055 and −0.062 at 128 tokens.

Filler does about as well as the real reasoning. Compared at the same length, the two are indistinguishable: repeated word −0.0059 (p = 0.48), pad token +0.0013 (p = 0.14). Gold reasoning is worth +0.0022 on these scenes, which is not itself distinguishable from the empty block here (standard error 0.0061).

The first token does most of the work. Going from an empty block to one arbitrary token is worth +0.0041 — about twice the whole gold-versus-empty effect. The model gives an empty reasoning block a probability of about 5×10−7, so most of what looks like a benefit of reasoning is the cost of that empty block, and one filler token removes most of it.

How much better is the true trajectory than a wrong one?

Score the true trajectory against a foreign one — another event’s future, a median 17 metres away — under identical conditioning. The gap between them is the separation: what the model gains from knowing which trajectory is right. This is the model doing its main job, and it is the scale the reasoning numbers should be read against.

Averaged over the 128 tokens it is +0.81 nats, a 2.25× probability ratio. That average is misleading, because the 128 positions are nothing like each other.

The first token alone carries 10.2 nats, a factor of 26,000. The median position carries 0.29 (1.33×) and the last carries 0.09. Ten of the 128 positions account for 56% of the total; an even spread would give 8%.

The reason is straightforward. The first trajectory token is the immediate acceleration, which is fixed by the current speed the model already has from the ego history. A trajectory taken from another scene starts at the wrong speed, so it is rejected immediately. Further out the real future is genuinely uncertain, and the gap between right and wrong falls to about a tenth of a nat.

The reasoning does not change any of this. The two curves coincide at every horizon, and the overall change is +0.0014 at p = 0.11. The only visible departure is a small negative dip at the first token — if anything the reasoning slightly reduces the model’s discrimination at the position where nearly all of it sits.

One consequence is worth carrying back to the reasoning numbers above: they are per-token averages over a horizon whose behaviour varies by two orders of magnitude from one end to the other. A single average is a poor summary of that.

Every effect as a share of the separation

The separation is the natural denominator for the whole study: it is what the model gains from knowing which trajectory is right. Every effect measured here, as a fraction of it:

† The two “reasoning present” rows are measured against an empty-CoC control that the model treats as near-impossible, so they are not safe to quote — see the caveat below. The separation is Alpamayo 1.5’s; no equivalent run exists for A2S, so its row borrows that denominator and is indicative only.

The caveat on the empty control

Every “presence” number on this page — gold reasoning against an empty reasoning slot — rests on the assumption that an empty slot is a configuration the model accepts. It is not. Measured directly, the probability the model assigns to the reasoning block closing immediately after it opens is:

log pprobability
close the block after real prose−0.0496%
close the block immediately (empty)−14.41 ≈5×10−7

The empty control is off-distribution by roughly seven orders of magnitude. The trajectory is still scored in a well-formed context, so the number is not meaningless — but it compares gold reasoning against a state the model never sees in training, and should be read as “gold versus something alien,” not “gold versus nothing.” The related claim that this reproduces a validated no-CoC evaluation mode is withdrawn: that mode is authored in this fork and was never validated upstream.

This does not touch the content results. Gold-versus-donor, the within-scene sweep and the directive flips all compare two filled reasoning slots, so they never invoke the empty state. The content null and the length findings stand independently of it; what it qualifies is the presence term and anything derived from it.

Navigation commands, the one channel with a directional effect

The same probe applies to route conditioning, which enters the prompt as a <|route_start|>Turn left in 12m<|route_end|> section rather than as reasoning prose:

llr_nav = log p(a* | v, nav) − log p(a* | v)

The denominator inverts the rule that governs the reasoning case. Dropping the command removes its delimiters too, and that is correct here: the no-route sequence is produced by re-tokenizing, and it comes out byte-identical to the older template that has no route component at all. Nothing is overwritten, so the marker artefact that invalidated the first version of this study cannot arise.

Over the full split — 2,071 events, commands derived from the ground-truth future — removing the route section costs +0.0018 nats per trajectory token (10% trimmed; the raw mean of +0.0032 overstates it, skew +1.33). Small, but unambiguous: p = 6×10−16, 56.4% of events positive.

And unlike the reasoning span, this is not a length effect. A turn command is 8 tokens and “Continue straight” is 4. At the reasoning span’s measured rate of 0.0012 nats per token, 8 tokens should buy +0.0098. Turns actually return +0.0011 to +0.0020 — five to nine times less. Route tokens are not worth what reasoning tokens are worth, so whatever nav is doing, it is not occupancy.

What it is doing shows up in the control channel. Splitting the effect by command and by channel gives the one clean dissociation in this study:

Turns · curvature
+0.0030
n=187 · p = 7×10−4
Turns · acceleration
−0.0004
n=187 · p = 0.52, nothing
Paired contrast
+0.0036
within-event · p = 4×10−3

A lateral instruction moves lateral control and leaves longitudinal control untouched, and the contrast holds within each event rather than only in aggregate. Straight commands behave the other way round — their effect sits in acceleration (+0.0042) — which is what “no turn is coming” ought to inform. The turn effect in curvature is 1.9× the straight effect in curvature, so it is not a generic consequence of adding tokens.

Removing the reasoning entirely does not change any of this: with cot_text="" in both passes the paired difference is −0.0006 at p = 0.43. So the route channel is not merely re-stating something the reasoning already said.

Three caveats that matter. The commands are oracles, derived from the ground-truth future because this split carries no route annotation — so this is a ceiling under a perfect route, not a deployable number. Turns are only 9% of the split, so the 187 turn events remain the least-powered part of the analysis.

The falsification test passed. Swapping left↔right on the same 187 turn events drops the curvature effect from +0.0030 to +0.0012, where it is no longer distinguishable from zero (p = 0.19), with a significant within-event paired difference (+0.0025, p = 0.023). Swapping retains 41%, and that remainder is not significant. The direction carries real information — this is the one conditioning channel in the study that behaves like information rather than compute.

What this means

The reasoning Alpamayo 1.5 produces is, as far as its own discrete-token trajectory head is concerned, decorative. The trajectory is predicted from vision and ego-motion, and the explanation rides alongside without feeding back into it. That is the shortcut this diagnostic was written to detect, and finding it is the useful outcome: it means there is a real target to aim at rather than an effect to preserve.

  • The content null is the robust part; the presence term is not. Three independent designs agree that content is zero — donors at full split, matched-length gold-versus-filler, and the within-scene sweep. The presence term has not held up as well: the empty block it is measured against is off-distribution by seven orders of magnitude, and one arbitrary filler token recovers about twice the whole effect. Read the headline as “content is zero”, and treat the occupancy figure as an artefact of its control until it is measured against an in-distribution baseline — minimal real prose rather than an empty slot. No run in this study uses one, and that is the main open gap on this head.
  • It sets up the regularizer rather than ruling it out. An auxiliary −β·L_LLR term would be creating a reasoning → action dependence, not reinforcing an existing one, and this is the quantity it should move. There is a full 0.27 nats of headroom before reasoning would matter as much as the camera feed does today.
  • It measures the discrete-token head, not the deployed one. The likelihood log p(a*) is only readable because this pathway emits trajectory tokens. The head actually shipped is a diffusion/flow-matching expert with no token logits, so carrying the result across needs a separate consistency formulation.
  • No model in this family is yet a counter-example. Alpamayo 2 Super, measured the same way over 2,070 events, gains eighteen times more from having its reasoning slot filled — but its content term is zero too (trimmed +0.0003, signed-rank p = 0.58). So A2S is not a demonstration that a trajectory head can attend to what its explanation says, and it cannot serve as the reference point this regularizer aims at. An earlier version of this page claimed the opposite, on the strength of a four-event probe that the full split reversed. What the two models establish together is narrower and more useful: the occupancy effect varies by 18× across the family while the content effect stays at zero in both. Creating a content dependence is an open problem, not a property to be transferred from a model that already has it.

Measured over reasoning/ood_reasoning.parquet (train + val, 2,071 of 2,077 events; 6 excluded by per-clip streaming failures) on Alpamayo-1.5-10B-rl-training via the discrete-token TrainableReasoningVLA pathway — 265,088 scored trajectory tokens across two forward passes each. Baseline log p(a*) is −1.932 nats per token. Alpamayo 2 Super measured identically via phase0_llr_per_token_a2s.py (128-token basis, empty denominator), with structural and control verification in phase0_llr_verify_setup_a2s.py. Method, controls and per-token output for 1.5: phase0_llr_per_token.py, phase0_llr_sanity_controls.py. Written up in results/phase0_llr_action_direction.md.
